documents.title: A Thorough View of Exact Inference in Graphs from the Degree-4 Sum-of-Squares Hierarchy

texts.raid-human: Performing inference in graphs is a common task within several machine learning problems, e.g., image segmentation, community detection, among others. For a given undirected connected graph, we tackle the statistical problem of exactly recovering an unknown ground-truth binary labeling of the nodes from a single corrupted observation of each edge. Such problem can be formulated as a quadratic combinatorial optimization problem over the boolean hypercube, where it has been shown before that one can (with high probability and in polynomial time) exactly recover the ground-truth labeling of graphs that have an isoperimetric number that grows with respect to the number of nodes (e.g., complete graphs, regular expanders). In this work, we apply a powerful hierarchy of relaxations, known as the sum-of-squares (SoS) hierarchy, to the combinatorial problem. Motivated by empirical evidence on the improvement in exact recoverability, we center our attention on the degree-4 SoS relaxation and set out to understand the origin of such improvement from a graph theoretical perspective. We show that the solution of the dual of the relaxed problem is related to finding edge weights of the Johnson and Kneser graphs, where the weights fulfill the SoS constraints and intuitively allow the input graph to increase its algebraic connectivity. Given an undirected connected graph and a single noisy observation of each edge, the goal is to exactly recover an unknown ground-truth binary labeling of the nodes. This problem can be cast as a quadratic combinatorial optimization over the Boolean hypercube, which is NP-hard in general, and is therefore commonly attacked by convex relaxations. The degree-2 relaxation from the sum-of-squares hierarchy, i.e., the standard semidefinite program, has been studied extensively and its exact recovery behavior is well characterized in terms of a spectral quantity of the graph. The degree-4 relaxation is provably tighter and succeeds in regimes where the degree-2 relaxation fails, but it is generally dismissed as computationally prohibitive, since it optimizes over a matrix whose dimension grows quadratically with the number of nodes. In this work we give a thorough view of the degree-4 case. We exploit the structure of the moment matrix to obtain a low-rank, Burer-Monteiro-style parameterization, and we analyze a projected gradient method over this non-convex landscape, establishing a per-iteration cost and a linear convergence rate to a solution from which the ground truth is read off. On the statistical side, we derive sufficient conditions for exact recovery that depend on the connectivity of the graph and on the noise level, and we show analytically that these conditions are weaker than the best known conditions for the degree-2 relaxation, quantifying the gain of moving one level up the hierarchy. We also clarify when the extra level does not help, characterizing graph families for which the two relaxations share the same recovery threshold. texts.raid-claude:
Deep learning has become the dominant paradigm for medical image segmentation, yet its success rests on large collections of voxel-wise annotations that are expensive to obtain, require clinical expertise, and generalise poorly across scanners, protocols and anatomies. Registration-based label propagation offers an appealing alternative, since a single annotated atlas can in principle segment an entire cohort by deforming its labels onto unlabelled scans. In practice, however, such approaches are limited by the objective that drives the registration: intensity-based similarity metrics are unreliable under low tissue contrast, intensity inhomogeneity and inter-subject variability, so the resulting deformation fields align appearance rather than anatomy, and propagated labels drift at structure boundaries.

In this work we introduce a contrastive registration framework for unsupervised medical image segmentation, which learns deformation and segmentation jointly without any ground-truth masks for the target images. Our key idea is to drive registration in a learned representation space rather than in intensity space: a contrastive objective pulls together the features of anatomically corresponding locations in the moving and fixed images while pushing apart features of distinct structures, yielding embeddings that are discriminative of anatomy and invariant to appearance. We couple this objective with a deformation model that aggregates non-local context, so that global anatomical layout constrains local correspondence, and with a consistency term that ties the propagated labels to the predicted segmentation.

We evaluate the framework on multi-centre cardiac MRI and abdominal CT benchmarks. The proposed method consistently improves over unsupervised registration, clustering and self-supervised segmentation baselines, approaches the performance of supervised models trained with limited annotation, and transfers across imaging centres without retraining. Ablation studies isolate the contribution of the contrastive objective, the non-local deformation model and the consistency term, and analyse robustness to atlas choice and to the number of negatives.

texts.raid-claude: Segmenting small and thin anatomical structures from clinical images is an ill-posed problem: the voxel size is of the same order as the structure itself, contrast is weak, and partial volume effects blur the boundaries. Statistical shape models are an effective way of regularizing such problems, but conventional model fitting returns a single point estimate and no measure of confidence, which is problematic when the resulting shape is used to derive clinical measurements. We introduce a Bayesian formulation of shape model inference based on a logistic shape representation. A shape is encoded implicitly by a signed distance-like function constrained to a low-dimensional linear subspace learned from a set of segmented surfaces, and a logistic transform maps that function to voxelwise membership probabilities. Image observations are then modeled as Bernoulli variables, which yields a likelihood that is smooth and differentiable with respect to both shape and pose parameters and that accounts explicitly for partial volume voxels rather than treating them as noise. Together with Gaussian priors on the shape coefficients and on the similarity transform, this defines a posterior distribution over shapes that we characterize with Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, using a Laplace approximation at the maximum a posteriori estimate to precondition the sampler. The framework also allows the intensity-to-probability mapping and the model hyperparameters to be estimated jointly with the shape. We apply the approach to cochlea segmentation from clinical computed tomography, where the scala tympani and scala vestibuli are not resolvable at the acquired resolution. The method achieves segmentation accuracy comparable to or better than deterministic shape model fitting and deep learning baselines, while additionally providing credible intervals on derived quantities such as cochlear duct length, a measurement used for electrode array selection in cochlear implant surgery. The posterior spread is shown to be informative, growing where the image evidence is weakest and correlating with the actual error of the estimate.

documents.title: Large-scale image segmentation based on distributed clustering algorithms

texts.raid-human: Many approaches to 3D image segmentation are based on hierarchical clustering of supervoxels into image regions. Here we describe a distributed algorithm capable of handling a tremendous number of supervoxels. The algorithm works recursively, the regions are divided into chunks that are processed independently in parallel by multiple workers. At each round of the recursive procedure, the chunk size in all dimensions are doubled until a single chunk encompasses the entire image. The final result is provably independent of the chunking scheme, and the same as if the entire image were processed without division into chunks. This is nontrivial because a pair of adjacent regions is scored by some statistical property (e.g. mean or median) of the affinities at the interface, and the interface may extend over arbitrarily many chunks. The trick is to delay merge decisions for regions that touch chunk boundaries, and only complete them in a later round after the regions are fully contained within a chunk. We demonstrate the algorithm by clustering an affinity graph with over 1.5 trillion edges between 135 billion supervoxels derived from a 3D electron microscopic brain image.

texts.raid-mistral-chat: Large-scale image segmentation is a challenging task in computer vision that involves dividing an image into multiple regions based on their visual characteristics. Distributed clustering algorithms offer a promising approach to this problem by allowing for parallel processing of image data across multiple nodes in a distributed system. In this paper, we propose a novel large-scale image segmentation method based on distributed clustering algorithms. Our approach involves dividing the image into smaller regions and applying a clustering algorithm to each region in parallel. The resulting clusters are then merged to form the final segmentation result. We evaluate our method on a large dataset of images and demonstrate its effectiveness in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Our results show that our method outperforms traditional centralized clustering algorithms and can scale to handle very large images.
texts.raid-claude: Image segmentation is a fundamental step in scene interpretation, but classical clustering-based formulations scale poorly: as image size grows from megapixels to gigapixels, the pixel- or object-level feature sets exceed the memory of a single machine, and the iterative distance computations that dominate clustering become prohibitively slow. This paper presents a distributed framework for segmenting very large images by reformulating clustering-based segmentation as a data-parallel computation. The image is decomposed into overlapping tiles that are distributed across a compute cluster, local features (spectral, textural, and spatial) are extracted in parallel, and cluster assignment and centroid update steps are expressed as map and reduce operations so that only compact sufficient statistics, rather than raw pixel data, are exchanged between nodes. To avoid the boundary artifacts introduced by naive tiling, we add a global centroid synchronization step and a border-region reconciliation procedure that merges segments spanning adjacent tiles under a region-adjacency criterion. We further reduce communication cost through scalable seeding and mini-batch updates. Experiments on high-resolution remote sensing and biomedical imagery show that the distributed implementation produces segmentations essentially equivalent to the centralized baseline, as measured by boundary recall and region consistency, while achieving near-linear speedup with the number of nodes and enabling the segmentation of images that cannot be processed on a single workstation.
